questions.q: State the three dominant gases in Earth's primordial atmosphere and their approximate combined percentage, contrasting with the two dominant gases in the present atmosphere.
questions.a: Primordial atmosphere: Hydrogen (H₂), Helium (He), Methane (CH₄), Ammonia (NH₃), and Water Vapour (H₂O) — H₂ and He together comprised >90% but escaped to space; the retained reducing gases (CH₄, NH₃, H₂O, CO₂) made up nearly 100% of the early secondary atmosphere. Present atmosphere: Nitrogen (N₂ ~78%) and Oxygen (O₂ ~21%) comprise 99%. A wrong answer (e.g., stating O₂ was present primordially) reveals the student conflates the secondary atmosphere with the modern one and misses the role of biological oxygen production.

questions.q: Explain why the primordial atmosphere's hydrogen and helium escaped to space, while nitrogen and carbon dioxide were retained, using the concepts of molecular mass, thermal velocity, and Earth's escape velocity.
questions.a: Hydrogen (2 g/mol) and helium (4 g/mol) have low molecular masses; at Earth's early high exospheric temperatures, their average thermal velocities exceeded Earth's escape velocity (11.2 km/s), allowing Jeans escape. Nitrogen (28 g/mol) and CO₂ (44 g/mol) are heavier, so their thermal velocities remain well below escape velocity, causing retention. A wrong answer (e.g., "gravity pulled heavier gases down") shows confusion between gravitational settling (which doesn't separate gases in a turbulent atmosphere) and thermal escape physics.

questions.q: Given that volcanic degassing releases H₂O (60%), CO₂ (20%), SO₂ (10%), N₂ (5%), and trace gases, calculate the approximate partial pressure of CO₂ in the early secondary atmosphere if total pressure was 100 bar, and explain why this did NOT lead to a runaway greenhouse like Venus.
questions.a: Step 1: Identify CO₂ fraction = 20% of total outgassed volatiles. Step 2: Total pressure = 100 bar (assumed for early dense atmosphere). Step 3: Partial pressure CO₂ = 0.20 × 100 bar = 20 bar. Step 4: Contrast with Venus: Earth's CO₂ dissolved in liquid oceans (once cooled) and was sequestered via carbonate-silicate weathering cycle (Urey reaction), while Venus lost its water to photodissociation and hydrogen escape, halting carbonate formation. A wrong answer (e.g., "Earth is farther from Sun") ignores the critical role of liquid water and plate tectonics in carbon cycling.

questions.q: Analyse the following statement: "The Great Oxidation Event (GOE) at 2.4 Ga was caused solely by the evolution of cyanobacteria." Identify two additional geological factors that controlled the timing and magnitude of atmospheric O₂ rise.
questions.a: The statement is incomplete. Factor 1: Tectonic burial of organic carbon — without subduction/burial of photosynthetic organic matter, O₂ would rapidly react with surface reduced minerals (Fe²⁺, S⁻²) and be consumed. Factor 2: Decline in mantle reduced gas flux (H₂, CH₄, CO) as Earth cooled — reduced volcanic gases act as oxygen sinks; their decline lowered the O₂ consumption rate. A wrong answer focusing only on biology misses the geochemical coupling between lithosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere that defines Earth system science.

questions.q: Evaluate the hypothesis that banded iron formations (BIFs) are direct evidence of the GOE. What does their disappearance after 1.8 Ga tell us about ocean chemistry and atmospheric O₂ levels?
questions.a: BIFs (alternating Fe₂O₃ and chert layers) formed when dissolved Fe²⁺ in anoxic deep oceans upwelled and met O₂-producing cyanobacteria at the surface, precipitating Fe³⁺ oxides. Their abundance 2.5–1.8 Ga indicates O₂ was locally produced but globally low (deep ocean remained anoxic). Their disappearance ~1.8 Ga signals deep-ocean oxygenation: once O₂ penetrated the deep ocean, Fe²⁺ oxidized before upwelling, ending BIF deposition. A wrong answer (e.g., "BIFs prove high O₂") confuses local oxidation with global atmospheric levels; BIFs actually require LOW global O₂ to transport Fe²⁺.

questions.q: Design a conceptual model (flowchart or annotated diagram) showing the carbon cycle feedback that stabilised Earth's climate during the faint young Sun paradox (30% less solar luminosity at 4 Ga), linking volcanic CO₂, silicate weathering, and carbonate precipitation.
questions.a: A good model includes: (1) High volcanic CO₂ → greenhouse warming → liquid oceans. (2) Warm, wet climate → enhanced silicate weathering (CaSiO₃ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + SiO₂). (3) Carbonate precipitation in oceans → CO₂ drawdown. (4) Cooling → reduced weathering → CO₂ buildup (negative feedback). Must show arrows for "increase/decrease" and label "thermostat". A poor model omits the temperature-weathering feedback loop or treats CO₂ as only a source, not a regulated variable.
